source: Tran and Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: At equal thinking-token budgets a single agent (SAS) was best or tied with best in most cells, but not at 100 tokens, and the average edge disappears at 10k. Gap 2: a crossover exists at both ends.
numbers: Models Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro; FRAMES and 4-hop MuSiQue; budgets 100/500/1k/2k/5k/10k. Mean accuracy SAS vs Sequential vs Debate vs Ensemble: 100: .290/.364/.370/.280; 1k: .418/.379/.388/.333; 5k: .427/.386/.420/.411; 10k: .411/.424/.423/.420. Gemini-2.5-Pro FRAMES at 100: SAS .368, Seq .654. Context corrupted (substitution alpha=.7): sequential beats SAS.
limits: Text-only multi-hop QA. Caps, not forced budgets. LLM judge from same family. Text says SAS best at all budgets except 100, but the 10k average favours Debate/Seq by about 1 point. Only the first 100k characters of the page were read. A public critic argues 10k is too small to need multi-agent.
agent_relevance: Under a small budget a staged or multi-agent split can beat one agent; at mid budgets one agent wins; at large budgets the methods tie. Single-agent baselines here are 0.25-0.69, so the 45% threshold is not tested cleanly.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Token budget was matched between single and multi-agent configurations. A capability-saturation interaction shows more agents hurt when the single-agent baseline is already high.
numbers: Matched total reasoning-token budget, mean 4,800 tokens per trial. Interaction PSA x log(1+agents) beta=-0.236, CI -0.396 to -0.076, p=.004; boundary about 0.45 raw accuracy. Above 45%: Workbench SAS .629 (MAS +5.6% to -1.2%), PlanCraft .568 (-39.1% to -70.0%), SWE-bench Verified .522 (-2.1% to -14.9%). Below 45%: Finance Agent .349 (+73.1% to +80.8%), BrowseComp-Plus .318 (+0.2% to +9.2%), Terminal-Bench .344 (Independent +1.7%, Centralized -19.2%). Overall mean MAS change -0.3% (CI -58.7% to +77.2%). Error amplification SAS 1.0, Independent 17.2, Decentralized 7.8, Hybrid 5.1, Centralized 4.4.
limits: Threshold is a fitted boundary over six benchmarks, not an experiment on one task at varied difficulty. Source reports inconsistent Finance Agent SAS values (0.349 vs 0.280 and 0.465). Only first 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is mostly closed for agentic tasks: at equal tokens MAS gains only where single-agent accuracy is low and the task decomposes. Our scaffolded single agent should be the default above about 45%.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups (composition of groups)
finding: The 108 groups were built from only 8 LLMs from 5 provider families, so the factor was not tested across truly independent model sets. Group members are reshuffled copies of the same 8 models.
numbers: Models: gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, gpt-4o-mini; Qwen2.5-7B, 32B, 72B; glm-4-9b-chat; internlm2_5-20b-chat; gemma-2-27b-it. Group sizes 3,5,8; rounds 2,3; topologies decentralized, centralized, random; homogeneous or heterogeneous. Five tasks: commonsense, maths, games, coding, writing. 108 groups in total.
limits: All from one 2024 debate framework (Du et al.), all groups under 10 agents, mostly small open models; the authors list these as limitations. Three of 8 models are the same Qwen family, so non-independence is high.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: no study yet draws groups from disjoint model sets. Shared base ability could produce the 66% factor.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups (predictors)
finding: Random forest puts collaboration process above member ability, with mean member g included, so there is partial control for mean capability. Prediction works on unseen groups.
numbers: Skill congruence over 50% of importance; average individual intelligence 37%; maximum individual intelligence, group size and effort each under 5%. 2-fold CV: R2 over 0.8 for ACI, over 0.6 on most tasks. Leave-one-task-out in a MAS optimiser. A group with 75% higher cost had 9.7% lower ACI.
limits: Random-forest importance with correlated predictors; skill congruence is computed from the same task scores, so it is partly circular. Not a regression with partial effects; no confidence intervals seen.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: mean g carries about a third of importance, process more than half, but circularity means do not rely on it.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench, structured protocol)
finding: A two-stage structured exchange lifts hidden-profile accuracy from near zero to about 0.73-0.80 across three models. Gap 7 closed for this benchmark.
numbers: Protocol: Exchange (2 rounds; each agent shares 1-2 decision-relevant facts and one reason the front-runner may be wrong) then Decide (1 pass; summarise evidence and uncertainty, vote). 18 HiddenBench tasks, 5 runs each, 4 agents. GPT-4.1 .037 -> .800; Gemini-2.5-Flash .173 -> .727; Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite .043 -> .743.
quote: does not assume prior knowledge of which information is missing or relevant
limits: Only 18 of 65 tasks. 90 runs per cell, no confidence intervals seen. Token or cost overhead not reported; about 3 passes versus the 5-20 rounds of the baseline. Protocol does not reveal which info is missing. Only first 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Direct hint for an inter-agent or memory step: force each member to state unique facts, then pool. Cost looks small (3 passes).

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) HiddenBench group-size table
finding: Gain from default talk shrinks as groups grow, at fixed GPT-4.1.
numbers: N=3 (7 tasks) pre .167 post .514; N=4 (58 tasks) .072 -> .321; N=5 (5) .116 -> .180; N=6 (5) .087 -> .283; N=7 (5) .017 -> .023. Full-profile accuracy near perfect throughout.
limits: Rows N=5-7 rest on 5 tasks each; task difficulty is confounded with size. Default talk setup, not the structured protocol.
agent_relevance: Supports K13: more members do not pool more. Do not add voices without a pooling step.

source: Graf, Gimpel, Barlow (2019) Clarifying the Structure of Collective Intelligence in Teams: A Meta-Analysis (CI 2019 abstract)
finding: Pooled task-type correlations are near zero and give three factors, not one. This is a 4-page work-in-progress abstract.
numbers: 745 teams, 13 studies, 6 papers, 128 correlations, MASEM with three-level mixed-effects regression. Pooled 5x5 matrix of McGrath task types: entries -0.17 to 0.17, average r=.001. One-factor CFA: chi2=40.79, df=5, CFI=.73, TLI=.45, RMSEA=.10. PAF: eigenvalue 1.05 (17%), second 15%; parallel analysis 3 factors (idea generation, conflict resolution, execution; Varimax loadings .89, .99, .90).
limits: Only 5 variables. Correlations are between task TYPES, each averaged over different concrete tasks, so a study's own tasks are mixed with other studies' tasks. The authors say the review is being updated. Not a full peer-reviewed paper. Woolley Study 2 is listed as 107 teams, not 152.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: the null may come from collapsing tasks into types and from pooling across face-to-face and computer-mediated contexts, not only from c being absent.

source: Graf, Gimpel, Barlow (2019) context moderator and task types
finding: The authors themselves say correlations are consistently larger face-to-face than computer-mediated, and they smooth this with one moderator across all matrix cells. Scoring rules were not modelled.
numbers: Context moderator coded face-to-face, online, hybrid, same coefficient for every cell. Task types covered: 2 (generate ideas), 3 (correct-answer problems), 4 (no right answer), 6 (conflicts of interest), 8 (execution); 3 of 8 McGrath types missing. Studies: Woolley 2010; Engel 2014 (32, 36); Engel 2015 (68, 25, 116); Barlow and Dennis 2016a (64, 65) and 2016b (86); Bates and Gupta (26, 40, 40).
limits: Task-type mix, medium and scoring are confounded across studies. No test separates them. Barlow and Dennis 2016b itself was not opened (paywalled, 403).
agent_relevance: For gap 6 the candidate causes are task-type collapse and medium; scoring rules remain untested. Our own factor test should use the same concrete tasks for every run.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (method)
finding: Riedl used a random-effects meta-analytic one-factor model on pooled correlations (weighted least squares), not Woolley's principal-axis eigenvalue share. Gap 4: no eigenvalue percentage is given in the main text.
numbers: 22 studies, 1,356 groups, 5,279 individuals, 4-8 tasks per study. Mean inter-item r=0.27 (0.12-0.50). Standardised loadings 0.27-0.52, average variance extracted 44%. Leave-one-task-out in each of eight tasks. CI score = average weighted z across tasks, scaled to mean 100, SD 15.
limits: Main text only (the SI with fit statistics was not read). The article was corrected in PNAS 2022; the correction was not read.
agent_relevance: Do not compare 44% AVE with Woolley's 43-44% eigenvalue share as the same quantity.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) arithmetic check of reported AVE
finding: Reported loadings and AVE do not match. If loadings lie between .27 and .52, the average squared loading is at most .27, so an AVE of 44% cannot come from these loadings. A one-factor model with mean r=.27 implies a first-factor share near 27%.
numbers: Max squared loading .52^2=.27. Under a one-factor model mean r equals mean squared loading, so .27. Rowe 2021 reports 30.23% over 49 loadings, which agrees with the lower figure.
limits: This is my arithmetic (inference), not a statement in the paper. AVE might be defined differently in the SI or corrected in 2022. Flag, do not assert error.
agent_relevance: Treat the human first-factor share in pooled data as about 27-30%, not 44%. That makes the LLM 66% figure about twice the human one, not 1.5 times.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people, Study 3 intervention (turn-taking and empathy instruction)
finding: The only randomised turn-taking intervention found in this search showed no effect on group scores. Gap 8 stays open for causal turn-taking effects.
numbers: 40 groups of 3 randomised after the main tasks: control n=14, empathy (equal talking time, attend to tone) n=14, authority (best-IQ member leads) n=12. Group Raven score. F(2,34)=1.14, p=.33. Beta authority -0.42 (95% CI -0.98 to 0.15, p=.142); empathy -0.13 (CI -0.68 to 0.41, p=.620).
limits: Tiny n, ceiling on Raven items suppressed variance (authors say so), manipulation applied once to ad hoc groups, no manipulation check on actual turn counts.
agent_relevance: No evidence that instructing equal turns raises scores. For agents: forced equal turns is untested.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) joint structural model of studies 2 and 3
finding: With latent-variable modelling (which handles task-level measurement error), average member IQ accounted for essentially all of group-IQ. This answers the measurement part of gap 5, but the study is not preregistered and the group tasks overlap IQ content.
numbers: Studies 2+3 combined, 80 groups of 3. Average IQ alone (Wonderlic) explained 81% of group-IQ variance, beta .86 (0.74-0.99). RME beta .191 (.032-.349, p=.019) when added to regression, but in SEM model A (RME only) fit was bad (CFI .601, RMSEA .312); model B IQ only CFI .955; best model D residual variance of group-IQ = 0, path fixed at 1.0 with no loss of fit (chi2(2)=0). Study 2 regression R2 .85 with IQ beta .74 (p=8.6e-9) and RME beta .3 (p=.003).
limits: Raven items hit ceiling in study 3. Group tasks included matrix-reasoning style tasks that overlap IQ content. Participants from one city (Chennai) and one student pool. Not preregistered.
agent_relevance: If Bates is right, c is average member ability. For LLM groups the matching claim is Zhou's mean-g effect (37%). Test it before claiming process effects.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Study 1 and power
finding: The replication attempt of Woolley found a single factor of 39.8% but no effect of proportion female or RME in Study 1, and power was limited.
numbers: Study 1: 26 groups; adjusted eigenvalues 1.98, .85, .69, .69, .79; single factor 39.8%; regression R2=.57, IQ beta .76 (p<.001), proportion female beta .12 (p=.447), RME beta -.11 (p=.520). Study 1 had 58% power to detect the reported .36 social-sensitivity effect; studies 2 and 3 combined 95%. Study 2: 40 groups of 3; no effect of proportion female (beta -.04, p=.57) or communication (beta -.07, p=.30).
limits: Study 1 used Raven for both individual IQ and one group task, which the authors note. Power computed for r=.36 from Woolley, larger than meta-analytic effects.
agent_relevance: A preregistered large replication (more than 150 groups, identical tasks, latent IQ) is still missing, so gap 5 stays open.

source: Tomprou, Kim, Chikersal, Woolley, Dabbish (2021) Speaking out of turn: how video conferencing reduces vocal synchrony and collective intelligence
finding: Randomised video vs audio manipulation raised speaking-turn inequality a lot, but CI did not differ significantly. Turn inequality acts through vocal synchrony, correlational mediation only.
numbers: 292 people assigned to 146 dyads; 99 dyads (198 people) analysed after audio failures: 49 audio-only, 50 video. CI video M=-.07 (SD .64) vs audio .08 (SD .53), t(97)=-1.23, p=.22. Turn inequality video 26.31 (SD 22.96) vs audio 9.14 (SD 5.63), t(97)=5.13, p<.001. Prosodic synchrony video -.32 vs audio .26, t(97)=-2.95, p=.004. Prosodic synchrony predicts CI b=.29, p=.003. Turn inequality predicts lower prosodic synchrony b=-.35, p=.001.
limits: Dyads only, one session, six TCI tasks; about a third of dyads lost; the manipulation changes many things besides turn-taking; mediation is statistical, not causal. Whether condition assignment was random is not explicit.
agent_relevance: Equal turns look like a marker of good coordination, not a lever. Forcing equal turns in LLM groups is untested.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models (main experiments)
finding: With 200 groups per arm, the theory-of-mind prompt did not change overall success. Its benefit rests on a marginal mediation, and the share of groups showing emergent coordination was lower under ToM.
numbers: GPT-4.1, N=10 agents, temperature 1, 200 groups per condition (Plain, Persona, ToM), 600 experiments. Text: overall success rate not significantly different across interventions. Mediation ToM->synergy->performance ACME=0.034, p=.053. Emergence capacity (groups with p<.05): 32% overall, Plain 37%, Persona 44%, ToM 18%. Preliminary grid: sizes 3-15, T 0-1 step .1, 50 groups per cell, 7,150 runs; OR .92 per member, OR 1.50 per unit temperature. Llama 8B largely failed; Llama 70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3-235B matched GPT-4.1.
limits: Single task (guessing game without direct communication). Temperature was NOT varied in the main arms, so the critique item about temperature confounding applies only to the preliminary grid. Last 17k characters of page not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 answer: an explicit perspective-taking prompt, run with adequate power (200 per arm), did not raise success. Do not add a 'what do others think' step to our schema on this evidence.

source: Li, Chen, Hou et al. (2023) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: Explicit belief-state text raised ToM inference accuracy and reduced invalid actions, but the team-level test used only three repeated trials per condition, so power is low.
numbers: Team of three agents in a bomb-defusal text game, temperature 0, three trials. ToM accuracy: ChatGPT introspection 79.0%, 1st-order 41.9%, 2nd-order 11.6%; GPT-4 80.0/60.0/64.3%; GPT-4+Belief 97.2/80.1/69.4%. Team-score table was not machine-readable in the PDF text.
limits: Three trials per condition at temperature zero cannot give a confidence interval. Single game. GPT-4 vs GPT-4+Belief differ in text state, not only in perspective-taking. Abstract claims improved task performance; the table was not read.
agent_relevance: Perspective tracking as a state variable (belief state) is cheap and helped inference. Evidence for score gains is below the 50-run threshold.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models (scope check)
finding: The 591-model factor is across models on public leaderboard tests, not across prompts or scaffolds on one model. Fine-tunes and merges of shared bases are included. So gap 9 (a scaffold factor) is untested by this paper.
numbers: 591 LLMs, 12 tests; mean r=0.73; general factor 65.6%; parameter count with factor r=0.54. The text discusses unique, fine-tuned and merged models and names parameter count as the only predictor examined.
limits: Non-independence of rows noted by the authors. One predictor only. No analysis of prompting strategy.
agent_relevance: A 'scaffold factor' (one agent, several scaffolds, many tasks) has no published test found here. Cheap to run ourselves.

source: Li et al. (2026) Superminds Test: actively evaluating collective intelligence of agent society (abstract page)
finding: A society of over two million agents on MoltBook showed no collective intelligence on probes: it did not beat single frontier models, rarely combined distributed information and often failed simple coordination.
numbers: Three tiers: joint reasoning, information synthesis, basic interaction. Platform over 2 million agents. Threads rarely went beyond one reply; most replies were generic or off topic.
limits: Abstract page only; model list, group sizes and numbers were not available.
agent_relevance: Scale without structured interaction gives no c. Adds a second null beside Riedl 2026.
